newsitem.title: CAMBODIA: Cambodia clamps down on illegal Chinese immigrants.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia clamps down on illegal Chinese immigrants.

text.p: Cambodian border police have cracked down on illegal ethnic Chinese immigrants following last month's swoop on a human smuggling syndicate in Phnom Penh, Cambodian Interpol officials said on Wednesday.

"We have strong measures, and near the Vietnam border we have sent many (ethnic) Chinese back. We are starting to control passports carefully," said Colonel Lam Buntha, deputy chief of Cambodia's Interpol office.
The international police agency is funded by the interior ministry and is separate from the police.
He and other police declined to say how many ethnic Chinese had been deported, but said most had crossed into Cambodia from Vietnam and were hiding in guest houses near the border.
Most of the immigrants appeared to be from mainland China, although some of the suspected traffickers are from Hong Kong.
The scale of Cambodia's human trafficking problems came to light on Christmas Day, when police uncovered 78 ethnic Chinese in a Phnom Penh villa.
The figure was revised from an earlier tally of 81.

The group included four suspected ringleaders of a sophisticated crime syndicate thought to have illegally moved Chinese immigrants to the United States, South America, Europe and Africa, police said.
Police found fake Chinese and Cambodian immigration stamps, 26 fake Chinese passports, a phone book listing suspected criminal contacts on three continents and drugs in the raid.
"This is not a small organisation and every day more people are flowing in," Police General Skadavy M. Ly Roun told Reuters.
He said there were about 10,000 illegal ethnic Chinese immigrants in Cambodia.
The four suspected syndicate ringleaders, including two men wanted in Hong Hong and one man wanted in China, were being held in Phnom Penh's T3 prison pending a court date, police said.
They said they did not know when the four men would appear in court, but that they expected them to receive sentences of a minimum of five years' jail on human trafficking charges.
Skadavy said police were cooperating with Interpol in Hong Kong and China on the investigation of the four men.
Nine of the ethnic Chinese, eight men and a woman, appeared in municipal court on Wednesday on charges of travelling without visas.
Nineteen others have already been sentenced to three months' jail for not having passports. They would be deported after serving their time, police said.
The remaining 46 people, seven women and 39 men, would be fined for carrying expired passports, Lam Buntha said.
Cambodia has been hard-pressed to tackle a growing human trafficking problem because of a lack of funds and lawlessness, police officials said.
